what: Internationalization (i18n) is building the app so any language, date format and text direction can plug in without code changes; localization (l10n) is supplying the actual translations and regional formats for each locale. The browser's Intl API and ICU message strings do most of the heavy lifting.
like: Like a classroom whiteboard with blank label slots: the layout is fixed once, and each language just fills in its own words, numbers and reading direction.
why: Reach new markets without forking the code
Plurals, dates, numbers and currency are different per language, and hand-rolled string code gets them wrong
RTL languages like Arabic and Hebrew need a mirrored layout, which is cheap if you plan for it early

steps.d: Pick it from the URL (/fr/...), a saved preference, or Accept-Language, and put it on the html element as lang and dir. Locale in the URL is best for SEO and sharing.
Each locale's messages are a separate chunk loaded on demand, so users download one language, not twenty.
Keep whole sentences with named placeholders and plural/select rules in ICU MessageFormat. Never build a sentence by joining pieces, because word order differs per language.
Intl.DateTimeFormat, NumberFormat, PluralRules, RelativeTimeFormat and ListFormat give locale-correct output from the browser's built-in CLDR data - no big library needed.
Set dir=rtl for right-to-left languages and write CSS with logical properties (margin-inline-start) so one stylesheet works both ways; flip directional icons by hand.
Extract keys from code, send to translators, and fail CI on missing keys. Pseudo-localization (long, accented fake text) finds clipped layouts before real translations arrive.

numbers.l: CLDR plural categories: zero, one, two, few, many, other (other is required in every language)
English uses two plural forms in the CLDR examples, Russian four (one, few, many, other)
Intl constructors on MDN's list (excluding DurationFormat): NumberFormat, DateTimeFormat, PluralRules, RelativeTimeFormat, ListFormat, Collator, Segmenter, Locale, DisplayNames

choices.t: Locale in URL, cookie or header
choices.d: URL prefix or subdomain is shareable and crawlable (add hreflang). Cookie or Accept-Language is invisible to links and search engines; use them only to suggest a redirect.
Intl covers formatting for free. You still need a library (FormatJS/react-intl, i18next, Lingui, next-intl) for message catalogs, ICU plurals and rich-text placeholders.
Bundle all locales (simple, huge), one chunk per locale (usual), or per-route namespaces (smallest, more requests). SSR must send the right messages to avoid a flash of the wrong language.
Logical properties (inline-start) make RTL nearly free. Physical left/right need per-direction overrides and are easy to forget.

instead.why: Bake RTL and text-expansion tolerance into shared components once
Locale in the URL is URL state: shareable, back-button friendly

breaks.d: 'You have ' + n + ' items' breaks plurals and word order in other languages.
breaks.see: Wrong plural forms or nonsense grammar in translated pages
breaks.fix: One ICU message per sentence with plural and select rules

breaks.d: German or Finnish text is longer than English and clips fixed-width buttons.
breaks.see: Cut-off labels in pseudo-locale or real translations
breaks.fix: Flexible layouts, no fixed widths on text, test with pseudo-localization

breaks.d: toLocaleString with the wrong locale, or a manual MM/DD/YYYY.
breaks.see: Dates read wrongly by users, 1,234.5 vs 1.234,5 confusion
breaks.fix: Always pass the user's locale to Intl formatters and store dates as UTC ISO

say: Messages live in per-locale catalogs using ICU MessageFormat, so plurals and word order are the translator's job, not string concatenation in code.
Dates, numbers, currency, lists and relative time go through the Intl APIs with the user's locale, and each locale's catalog is a lazy-loaded chunk.
We set lang and dir on the root and use CSS logical properties, so right-to-left is one stylesheet, and the locale lives in the URL for SEO and sharing.

followups.q: How do plurals work across languages?
followups.a: CLDR defines up to six categories per language (zero, one, two, few, many, other). ICU messages declare a branch per category and Intl.PluralRules picks the right one, so English needs two forms but Russian needs more.
Set dir=rtl and lang on html, use logical CSS properties, mirror directional icons and animations, and keep numbers and Latin snippets correct with bidi isolation where needed.

followups.q: How do you avoid a flash of the wrong language with SSR?
followups.a: Resolve the locale on the server from the URL, render with that locale's messages, and ship the same catalog to the client for hydration.

today: Intl is available across modern browsers and keeps adding formatters (DurationFormat is on MDN's list), so Intl-only formatting is normal. ICU MessageFormat remains the standard translator-facing syntax, supported by FormatJS and others.

check.q: Why not build 'You have N photos' by string concatenation?
check.a: Plural rules and word order differ by language
check.why: Whole-sentence ICU messages let translators handle plural categories and order.

check.q: How can one stylesheet serve both LTR and RTL layouts?
check.a: Use CSS logical properties and the dir attribute
d: Duplicate the CSS and swap files with a build flag
check.why: margin-inline-start and similar properties resolve against the writing direction.

check.q: Which is required in every language's CLDR plural rules?
check.why: Other is the catch-all form that every language defines.
